h.select_rule: Choose hypotheses with a clear causal mechanism, a large expected change in the edit's effect, and support from retrieved evidence or well-established principles such as diminishing returns, redundancy, or bottlenecks. Reject any whose direction hinges on subtle trade-offs.
h.strategy: Use retrieved findings about which components interact and which are redundant or critical. Build hypotheses around robust interaction patterns: an edit has less effect when its target is bypassed or redundant, and more effect when its target is the only or limiting pathway. Removal effects are stronger when there is little remaining alternative capacity. Propose diverse hypotheses across different edit types and conditions, each with a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: If edge 0 is none, node 1 receives no signal, so a conv on 1->3 does nothing.
Edge 1->2 is dead when node 1 has no input, so the edit cannot help.
A skip from a dead node 1 carries nothing, so the gain from adding it vanishes.
Node 2 only reaches the output through edge 5, so a conv on 0->2 is wasted if edge 5 is none.
Edge 1's output is disconnected from the output node when edge 5 is none, so the edit has no effect.
Edge 1->2 feeds only node 2, which is a dead end when edge 5 is none.
A direct skip already provides a bypass to the output, so extra conv capacity on 1->3 is partly redundant.
The direct skip carries the signal already, reducing the marginal value of a conv on 2->3.
A second shortcut adds little when a direct skip already exists, so the gain is smaller.
With no direct edge, edge 5 is a main route to the output, so removing it is more damaging.
